limitations: One engine-assisted reviewer. Ordinary root variations and played-move probes reviewed before neural rankings or extra-choice evidence. No consensus adjudication.

cases.rationale: C-file activity is the common issue. Rfc8, Rxf1+ followed by Rc8, and Ba6 all reach near-equal rook exchanges.
Rd2 and Rhf1 bring the second rook into play and Kb1 secures the king. The tested Rh5 stays viable, so the sacrifices do not establish a tactical requirement.
Rxe8 forces mate. The queen and rook exchanges after Rc1+ and Qc8 give a concrete mating route. Rxc6 wins a different material sequence.
White's active rook and central king control Black's pawn advance across Re7+, Rc7 and Kc3. The displayed lines offer no clear tactical contrast.
Kf2 limits the immediate attack. Ke2 and Ke4 allow Qg2+ and Re8+ before White can coordinate queen and rook.
Qc1+ gains the initiative and opens Qd2. Taking the knight instead permits f6+ and a sustained king attack.
The queen's raid on b4 runs into Rb8 and the d-file exchange. Qb6 lets White remove e4 immediately. Other lines do not settle on a single long-term advantage.
White has to remove the d1 rook. Qh6 allows Rxf1+ and Be5, while the two captures on d1 leave materially different but defensible lines.
Black can relocate the queen to support rook activity or advance the d-pawn. Comparable scores and different captures give insufficient evidence of a required forcing sequence.
The sacrifice on h6 allows immediate queen and rook captures, and e3 still lets White take b8 with check. Removing the b6 rook is the recurring urgent issue.
axb5 changes the position immediately. Kc7 allows Bxc5 and a pawn break, and Kb7 exposes the bishop on d6 to Rxd6 with check resources for Black.
White can centralize the queen and improve the knight or change the heavy-piece alignment along the open files. The played Nc3 stays close in value and the reply evidence differs.
Rook checks and attacks on a4 preserve approximate equality. The defensive placements manage the pawn targets through several viable move orders.
White's active king and bishop place pressure on two pawn fronts. Black has several similar methods of restraining White's kingside pawns and none changes the assessment sharply.
White can centralize the king or advance f5. The open c-file and access to better bishop squares matter across equivalent lines.
White improves the rooks and keeps pressure on the advanced f-pawn. Nd3 repeatedly hits the f4 rook but the independent variants do not establish a lost or won piece.
White can defend through several rook placements while keeping the king active against the opposing rook. The checks and temporary pawn targets preserve equality.
fxe5 changes the central pawn structure immediately. Be3 permits b4 with tempo against the knight, and Bxe5 gives Black the active Qb7 and bishop exchanges.
The capture on b4 changes the queenside structure. The alternative cxb4 allows Rxa3 and Bxf2+ as a concrete answer to Bxe5.
Black must develop and manage the king while White retains the f-pawn advance. The viable candidates reorganize the queen and bishop without confirming one forcing answer.
Bg4 meets kingside pressure by attacking the d1 rook. Bd7 allows another order with Bxc4 and Bxd1, while Qf8 favours queenside pawn counterplay.
Rb7+ repeatedly forces Ka2 and gives Black access to f2. The rook exchanges or checks depend on White's specific first move.
The forcing capture on f7 and then g6 changes the fate of the knights. Be3 permits Re7 and Nd5 as a materially different defensive line.
Bxc1 removes the bishop pair and lets Nf6 restrain the passer. The other moves allow the bishops to take better squares. The immediate tactical mechanism is unclear.
Both sides are choosing where to advance on opposite wings. Black's a-pawn can pull White's queenside apart while White's h-pawn displaces the bishop.
cxb6 eliminates the advanced pawn and makes Qxd3 answerable by e4 against the knight. The other viable lines balance the c7 promotion threat with central counterplay.
fxe4 preserves the rook on d8 from capture. dxe4 opens that file to Rxd8, and Qxe4 leaves fewer useful forcing options.
Rxg8 reduces the kingside pressure. Qe2 and Qf3 allow specific rook invasion and exchange sequences on g2 or g1 with the king exposed.
Bxd6+ removes the knight with tempo. The two alternatives permit Kf4, and only Rh3+ creates a concrete forcing continuation after the knight takes f5.
Advancing the d-pawn restricts the king and permits d2+ followed by Rxg3. The other move orders coordinate the rook and king at the cost of giving White time to advance h5.
